Maladaptive Strategies.value: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Fire/flame cues are hard to reconcile with a childhood domestic-violence witnessing trauma profile when the rest of the trigger, memory, threat, and appraisal items do not suggest fire, arson, or burn-related trauma content. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
issues.explanation: 'No longer capable of doing the things that defined me' suggests a loss of prior adult identity/functioning that is difficult to fit with a 19-year-old whose index trauma was childhood witnessed domestic violence. The other appraisals center on helplessness and failed protection, which fit better; this item is comparatively implausible for the developmental context.

vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a nineteen-year-old Latina woman who works as a train conductor on a commuter line in the greater Chicago area. She presented for treatment following what she described as a period of "not being able to keep it together anymore," though she had been living with the consequences of her childhood for most of her life.

Valentina grew up in a two-bedroom apartment on the southwest side of the city, the eldest of three children. From the time she was approximately seven until she was fourteen, she witnessed her stepfather assault her mother on a near-nightly basis. The violence followed a pattern she came to know with terrible precision: the apartment would grow quiet after dark, then would come the sound of the front door slamming, followed by shouting that escalated quickly into something physical. She would lie in the darkness of the room she shared with her younger siblings, her heart hammering against her ribs, pressing herself against the wall as though she could disappear into it. She remembers one particular night when she was ten - a night that has never fully become the past for her - when she crept to the doorway and watched her stepfather throw her mother against the kitchen cabinets. She could taste the metallic fear in her mouth, the same taste that returns to her now without warning. She did not call for help. She did not step into the kitchen. She stood frozen, and then she went back to bed.

In the years that followed, Valentina developed a way of moving through the world that was organized almost entirely around not stopping. She graduated high school early, earned her conductor's certification at eighteen, and threw herself into shift work with a focus that her supervisors admired. Keeping busy had always felt like the only reliable way to keep the past from catching up with her. She also began restricting what she ate, in a quiet, controlled way that she did not discuss with anyone - a way of managing something internal that felt otherwise unmanageable. When she had time to herself, she found her mind returning again and again to the question of what would have happened if her stepfather had never entered their lives, cycling through alternative histories that offered no resolution.

At work, Valentina operates the evening and overnight commuter runs, which means she regularly moves through tunnels and unlit stretches of track where the cab goes dark. In those moments, her heart begins to race, and the sensation of her own pulse is enough to pull her back to that bedroom - not as a memory she is recalling, but as something happening now, disordered and immediate, the sequence of events scrambled so that she cannot always tell what came before what. She cannot always say whether she is nineteen or ten. She has developed a habit of checking the cab door lock multiple times before a run begins and again at each stop, and she sleeps during the day with every window latch confirmed before she will lie down. Nights, even in her own apartment, do not feel safe to her. When a train on an adjacent platform brakes suddenly and the sound cracks through the station, she goes rigid, her body scanning for what is coming.

What frightens Valentina most, in a way she has never said aloud to anyone, is her certainty that she is the reason the violence happened - that something in how she behaved as a child invited or prolonged it. Alongside this sits the conviction that she failed her mother and her siblings in that kitchen doorway, and the broader belief that bad things will continue to find her because she is the kind of person they find. She has come to understand her own helplessness as a fixed feature of her life rather than a response to an impossible childhood situation.

She sought help after a night run during which she sat frozen at the controls for nearly a minute following an unexpected loud noise from the track, unable to distinguish where she was in time. A colleague had to speak to her twice before she responded. She came to the intake appointment hoping, she said quietly, to find out whether she was still fixable - and afraid, above everything else, of what the answer might be.
